'''Humphry John Moule Bowen''' (22 June 1929 – 9 August 2001) was a British [[botanist]] and [[chemist]].<ref name=":0">{{cite news|url=http://www.jpbowen.com/publications/hjmb-obituary.html |title=Obituary: Humphry Bowen |newspaper=[[The Times]] |date=28 August 2001 |accessdate=4 June 2013 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071202071551/http://www.jpbowen.com/publications/hjmb-obituary.html |archivedate=2 December 2007 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2001/oct/17/guardianobituaries.highereducation | title=Humphry Bowen: Practical botanist and chemist exploring the natural world | first=J. Michael | last=Moffatt | newspaper=[[The Guardian]] | date=17 October 2001 | access-date=4 June 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1339494/Humphry-Bowen.html | title=Obituaries: Humphry Bowen | newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]] | date=5 September 2001 | accessdate=4 June 2013}}</ref><ref name="independent">{{cite news | url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/humphry-bowen-729440.html | title=Obituaries: Humphry Bowen | newspaper=[[The Independent]] | date=25 September 2001 | accessdate=6 October 2011}}{{dead link|date=August 2021|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| first=S. L. | last=Jury | url=http://www.herbarium.rdg.ac.uk/modules.php?name=Collectors&rop=show_collector&id=12 | title=Humphry John Moule Bowen (1929–2001) | journal=[[Watsonia (journal)|Watsonia]] | volume=24 | pages=268–270 | year=2002 }}</ref>{{overcite|date=October 2024}}

== Early life and education ==
Bowen was born in [[Oxford]], son of the chemist [[Edmund Bowen]] and Edith Bowen (nee Moule).<ref name="symonds">{{cite book | title=The Changing Faces of North Oxford: Book One |publisher=Robert Boyd Publications | author=Symonds, Ann Spokes | chapter= Families: The Bowens | pages=81–83 | isbn=1-899536-25-6}}</ref> He attended the [[Dragon School]], gaining a scholarship to [[Rugby School]] and then a [[demyship]] to [[Magdalen College, Oxford]]. He won the ''Gibbs Prize''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ox.ac.uk/feesandfunding/ugcurrent/other/prizes/gibbs/ |title=Gibbs Prizes |publisher=[[University of Oxford]] |location=UK |accessdate=14 June 2014 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714223515/http://www.ox.ac.uk/feesandfunding/ugcurrent/other/prizes/gibbs/ |archivedate=14 July 2014 }}</ref> in 1949 and completed a [[Doctor of Philosophy|DPhil]] in [[chemistry]] at [[Oxford University]] in 1953 before starting his professional career as a chemist. Bowen was also a proficient amateur actor in his early years, appearing with a young [[Ronnie Barker]] at Oxford.<ref name=":0" />

== Research career ==
His first post was with the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] (AERE) near the village of [[Harwell, Oxfordshire|Harwell]] where he lived, working at the [[Wantage]] Research Laboratory, then in [[Berkshire]].<ref name=":1" /> His early work started an interest in [[radioisotopes]] and [[trace elements]] that he maintained throughout his working life. While at AERE, he spent several months in 1956 attending the [[British nuclear tests at Maralinga]] in Australia to study the environmental effects of [[radiation]].<ref name=":1" />

[[File:Bowen's Kale.jpg|thumb|upright|A jar of the botanical reference material [[Bowen's Kale]], in the collection of the [[Museum of the History of Science]], [[University of Oxford]], England.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/collections/imu-search-page/record-details/?TitInventoryNo=14609&querytype=field&thumbnails=on&irn=30882 | title=Jar of Bowen's Kale (Botanical Reference Material), Prepared by H. J. M. Bowen, 1960s | publisher=[[Museum of the History of Science]] | location=Oxford | accessdate=18 January 2015 }}</ref>]]
Bowen realized that the [[calibration]] of different instruments intended to measure [[trace elements]] was an important issue that needed addressing. His solution was to produce a good supply of a material which later become known as ''[[Bowen's Kale]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Katz |first=S. A. |date=January 2002 |title=Bowen's Kale: A brief review dedicated to the late Professor Humphry John Moule Bowen, 1929–2001 |journal=[[Journal of Radioanalytical and Nuclear Chemistry]] |volume=251 |pages=3–5 |doi=10.1023/A:1015021823497 |number=1 |bibcode=2002JRNC..251....3K |s2cid=93854964}}</ref> This was a dried, crushed chomogenate of the plant [[kale]], that was stable and consistent enough to be distributed as a research calibration standard - probably the first successful example of such a standard.<ref name="independent" />

In 1964, he was appointed as a lecturer in the chemistry department at the [[University of Reading]]. Later he was promoted to Reader in [[analytical chemistry]] in 1974. At Reading, Bowen undertook consultancy for [[Dunlop Rubber|Dunlop]], investigating potential uses for their products.<ref name=":0" /> When the ''[[Torrey Canyon]]'' oil disaster occurred in 1967, he realized that it might be possible to use foam booms to block the oil from spreading in the [[English Channel]]. His original experiments were conducted in a small bucket in his laboratory.<ref name=":1" /> Although not entirely successful in reality at the time due to the rough seas, this lateral thinking combined his interest in chemistry with his love of nature and has since been effectively deployed to protect ports and harbours against encroaching oil slicks. Bowen wrote a number of professional books in the field of chemistry, including two editions of ''[[Trace elements]] in [[Biochemistry]]'' (1966 and 1976).<ref>{{cite web| url=https://openlibrary.org/a/OL1636071A/H.-J.-M.-Bowen | title=H. J. M. Bowen | publisher=[[Open Library]] | accessdate=13 June 2014 }}</ref>

In 1968, Bowen noted that the paint used for [[Yellow line (road marking)|yellow line road markings]] can contain [[Chromate and dichromate|chromate]] pigment, which may cause [[urban pollution]] as it deteriorates.<ref name=":2">{{cite journal| last=Bowen | first=H.J.M. | title=Urban Pollution | journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume=218 | page=106 | date=6 April 1968 | issue=5136 | doi=10.1038/218106c0 | doi-access=free | bibcode=1968Natur.218..106B }}</ref> He pointed out that [[hexavalent chromium]] in dust can cause [[dermatitis ulceration]] on the skin, inflammation of the [[nasal mucosa]] and [[larynx]], and [[lung cancer]].<ref name=":2" />

From 1951 onwards, Bowen was a long-serving member of the [[Botanical Society of the British Isles]] (BSBI). He was meetings secretary for a period and the official recorder of plants for the counties of [[Berkshire]] and [[Dorset]], producing [[Flora (plants)|Floras]] for both counties.<ref name="berkshire-flora">{{cite book| first=H. J. M. | last=Bowen | title=The Flora of Berkshire | publisher=[[Holywell Press]] | location=Oxford | year=1968 }}</ref><ref name="dorset-flora">{{cite book|first=H. J. M. |last=Bowen |url=http://www.naturebureau.co.uk/shop/books/Dorsetflora.html |title=The Flora of Dorset |publisher=Pisces Publications |year=2000 |isbn=1-874357-16-1 |url-status=bot: unknown |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20060902220036/http://www.naturebureau.co.uk/shop/books/Dorsetflora.html |archivedate=2 September 2006 }}</ref> He retired to [[Winterborne Kingston]] in Dorset at the end of his life. He was also one of the leading contributors of botanical data for the ''Flora of Oxfordshire''.<ref>{{cite book| first1=John | last1=Killick | first2=Roy | last2=Perry | first3=Stan | last3=Woodell | authorlink3=Stan Woodell | title=Flora of Oxfordshire | publisher=Pisces Publications | year=1998 | isbn=1-874357-07-2 }}</ref> He acted as an expert botanical guide on tours around Europe, especially [[Greece]] and [[Turkey]].<ref name=":1" />

Humphry Bowen donated a large collection of [[lichen]]s from Berkshire and [[Oxfordshire]] to the [[Museum of Reading]] in the 1970s.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.collectionsgateway.org.uk/collections/47/collection%20lichen%20general.pdf | first=David | last=Notton | title=The Bowen collection of Lichens at Reading Museum | publisher=Collections Gateway | location=UK | accessdate=14 June 2014 }}</ref> He established the Bowen Cup at the University of Reading in 1988, an annual prize for the student in the Department of Chemistry at the University who achieves the top marks in Part II Analytical Chemistry.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.reading.ac.uk/chemistry/News/chem-news.aspx | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110911004455/https://www.reading.ac.uk/chemistry/News/chem-news.aspx | url-status=dead | archive-date=2011-09-11 | title=Bowen Cup for Analytical Chemistry 2010 | work=Chemistry: News | location=UK | date=2010 | accessdate=11 September 2011 }}</ref>
